name: two-time-constants
html:
Why the decay has two time constants

Figure 1 fits the signal with two exponentials. Here is where they come from, in four steps, with nothing assumed but first-order kinetics.

The model

Light puts the molecule in S2. It leaks to S1 at rate $k_1$, and S1 returns to the ground state at rate $k_2$:

$$\mathrm{S_2} \xrightarrow{\;k_1\;} \mathrm{S_1} \xrightarrow{\;k_2\;} \mathrm{S_0}$$

The derivation

1
Nothing feeds S2, so it simply empties: $$\frac{dP_2}{dt} = -k_1 P_2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad P_2(t) = e^{-k_1 t}.$$
2
S1 fills from S2 as it empties to S0: $$\frac{dP_1}{dt} = k_1 P_2 - k_2 P_1 = k_1 e^{-k_1 t} - k_2 P_1.$$
3
Multiply by $e^{k_2 t}$, integrate from $0$ with $P_1(0) = 0$: $$P_1(t) = \frac{k_1}{k_2 - k_1}\left(e^{-k_1 t} - e^{-k_2 t}\right).$$
4
The signal is a sum of what each state absorbs, so it is two exponentials: $$S(t) = a\,P_2 + b\,P_1 = A\,e^{-t/\tau_1} + B\,e^{-t/\tau_2}, \qquad \tau_1 = \frac{1}{k_1},\; \tau_2 = \frac{1}{k_2}.$$

What it means

The fast constant, $\tau_1$, is how long S2 lasts; the slow one, $\tau_2$, is how long S1 lasts. One exponential would be enough only if a state were skipped. The rates come from the states the paper's Equation (1) describes:
